summary: This standards-track RFC specifies how SIP, SDP and RTP deliver real-time media and metadata from a communication session to a recording device. It sets up a Recording Session between a Session Recording Client on the call path and a Session Recording Server.

eli5.summary: Like quietly passing a copy of a phone call to a tape machine, along with notes about the call.

questions: how does sip call recording work
what is the sdp record attribute
subtitle: How a call-path device streams a copy of a live call, plus notes about it, to a recording server using SIP, SDP and RTP.

tldr.problem: Call recording needs a standard way for a device on the call path to hand the call's media and descriptive information to a recorder, and to tell participants that recording is happening.
tldr.mechanism: The Session Recording Client opens a separate SIP session, the Recording Session, to the Session Recording Server. It sends copies of the media over RTP, sends metadata in SIP bodies, and signals recording state to participants with the SDP record and recordpref attributes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7866 is a Proposed Standard that covers active recording only. It has been updated by RFC 9806.

today: RFC 7866 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9806. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7866 specifies how to record a Communication Session (CS) by delivering its real-time media and metadata to a recording device. It follows the architecture in RFC 7245, uses the metadata format of RFC 7865, and is meant to satisfy the SIPREC requirements in RFC 6341. The protocol uses SIP, SDP and RTP to set up a Recording Session (RS) between a Session Recording Client (SRC), which is on the path of the CS, and a Session Recording Server (SRS) at the recording device.

The document considers only active recording, where the SRC purposefully streams media to the SRS and all participating user agents are notified of the recording. Passive recording, where a device picks up media from the network by port mirroring, is out of scope, and so is lawful intercept. It also leaves out which calls to record, recording and retention policies, searching and playing back recordings, and the policies for making users aware of recording. User agents need not be recording aware to take part in a CS that is being recorded.
sections.eli5: This document explains how to make a copy of a phone call for a recorder, and how to let people know they are being recorded. It does not decide which calls should be recorded.

sections.title: How Recording Sessions Work
sections.content:
The CS and the RS are independent SIP sessions. A SIP Back-to-Back User Agent (B2BUA) with SRC functionality can route a call between two user agents, relay their media, open an RS to the SRS and send replicated media there. An endpoint can also be its own SRC. In a centralized conference, the conference focus can provide the SRC function and may mix all the participants into one stream for the SRS. The SRC can choose when to establish the RS, independent of the CS.

One RS can record several CSs: each time the SRC wants to record a new call it sends a new SDP offer to add streams and updates the metadata. An SRS can also establish an RS to an SRC, although how it would choose calls to record is beyond the scope of the document.

Metadata travels as SIP message bodies. The SRC may put an initial snapshot in the first INVITE and send later changes in UPDATE or re-INVITE requests, normally as incremental updates. The SRS can ask for a fresh snapshot if it loses track of the updates.
sections.eli5: The phone call is one conversation, and the recording is a second, separate conversation where a copy of the first one is passed to the recorder.

sections.title: SIP Procedures
sections.content:
An RS is a SIP session with a few markers added. The SRC starts it by sending an INVITE to the SRS. The SRC MUST include the +sip.src feature tag in its Contact URI, and an SRS that starts an RS MUST include +sip.srs. Each side treats a session as an RS only when it sees the other side's feature tag together with the siprec option tag. The initiator MUST put siprec in the Require header, so a user agent that does not understand it rejects the INVITE with a 420 (Bad Extension) response.

Participants in the recorded call have their own markers. A user agent that supports recording indications adds the record-aware option tag to the Supported header of its initial INVITE or response. Such a recording-aware user agent MUST show the user whether recording is on, off or paused for each medium. Automatons without a user interface, such as IVR systems or PSTN gateways, SHOULD render the indication by other means, such as an in-band tone or a log entry.

If a participant is not recording aware, the SRC MUST still provide recording indications through other means, such as playing a tone in-band or having a signed participant contract in place.
sections.eli5: The recorder and the call-path device each wear a name badge saying what they are. If someone does not understand the badge, they politely refuse to join, so nobody is recorded by accident.

sections.title: SDP Handling, Indications and Preferences
sections.content:
The SRC and SRS follow the SDP offer/answer model. Since the SRC does not expect media back, it typically marks each stream a=sendonly, and the SRS answers a=recvonly. The SRC MUST put an a=label attribute on each recorded stream so the stream can be matched to the metadata. To remove a recorded stream, the offer sets its port to zero. To pause streaming, the SRC offers a=inactive and later goes back to a=sendonly. An SRS that is not ready to record can answer inactive and later send a new offer with a=recvonly. The SRS MUST NOT add recorded streams, and when it starts an RS it MUST send its INVITE without an SDP offer so the SRC can supply the streams.

Two new SDP attributes carry state in the recorded call itself. The SRC uses a=record with the values on, off or paused to tell recording-aware participants what is happening. A participant can state a preference with a=recordpref, with values on, off, pause or nopreference. Both can appear at session or media level, and media level overrides session level. Whenever the indication changes, the SRC MUST send a re-INVITE or UPDATE.

A preference is only a request. The SRC honors it according to local policy, and if it changes the recording state it MUST report the new state in a=record. A participant who does not want to be recorded but is notified anyway can avoid recording only by leaving the session.
sections.eli5: A little light on the call says "recording", "not recording" or "paused". You can ask the person running the recorder to turn it off, but they decide whether to listen.

sections.title: Carrying Media with RTP
sections.content:
The RTP section is largely guidance on using RTP and RTCP predictably. RTCP support is REQUIRED. The RECOMMENDED profiles are RTP/SAVPF for encrypted media and RTP/AVPF for unencrypted media, though implementations should not rely entirely on them for core functions. When sending RTP and RTCP, symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP are REQUIRED. For media that sits inactive for long periods, the SRC, SRS and recording-aware user agents are RECOMMENDED to use the keepalive procedure of RFC 6263 to hold open NAT bindings. The document also covers video recovery messages (FIR, PLI and TMMBR). The SRS MUST support both FIR and SIP INFO for fast video update, using FIR when it was negotiated.

How the SRC relays media depends on its role, and the SRC can play a different role in the RS than in the CS. As a translator it keeps each source's SSRC and passes RTCP reports through. As a mixer it combines streams under its own SSRC and lists the contributors as CSRC values. As an endpoint it runs an RTP session with the SRS that is completely independent of the CS. In all roles the SRC SHOULD map each unique CNAME in the CS to a unique CNAME in the RS.

For base interoperability, an SRC MUST support separate SDP m-lines, one per CS media direction. An SRS that records audio MUST accept separate audio m-lines, one per direction, so a typical audio call needs at least two audio m-lines at the SRS. An audio and video call needs at least four m-lines in total.
sections.eli5: The device in the middle can pass along each speaker's voice as its own track, blend everyone into one track, or run a brand new recording line. The recorder must at least understand the one-track-per-direction way.

sections.title: Recording Metadata
sections.content:
Metadata describes the recorded media and the CS it came from. Some of it lives in the SDP, and the rest is carried in a new content type, application/rs-metadata, with the Content-Disposition value recording-session. The XML format itself is defined in RFC 7865.

The SRC MUST send metadata and SHOULD send it as soon as it is available and whenever it changes. It is either a full snapshot of everything about the RS, or a partial update, which the SRC MAY send only after a full snapshot has been sent. The SRC SHOULD include a full snapshot in the initial INVITE. Metadata goes in INVITE, UPDATE, or the 200 response to an offerless INVITE from the SRS. When a message holds both an SDP offer and metadata, the body MUST be multipart/mixed, and a request whose metadata refers to SDP labels MUST include the offer that defines them.

The SRS has to keep track of the updates. If it loses state, it can send an UPDATE with a recording-session body, no SDP, and a request for a snapshot. The SRC MUST then immediately send a full snapshot in a separate INVITE or UPDATE. If the SRS finds syntax or semantic errors in the metadata, it can simply end the RS instead of asking again.

Persistent recording is the case where an RS exists without any CS. The SRC keeps the recorded streams ready, so a new CS only needs a metadata update, and it follows the keepalive recommendations of RFC 6263 to hold NAT bindings.
sections.eli5: Metadata is the notes that go with the recording: who was on the call and which track is whose. The first message is a full set of notes, later messages only say what changed, and the recorder can ask for a fresh full set.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because an RS is a standard SIP dialog, it can reuse existing SIP security mechanisms. The SRC and SRS MUST support SIP over TLS version 1.2, and the RS MUST be at least as secure as the CS. For example, if the CS uses SIPS and RTP/SAVP, the RS may not fall back to plain SIP or plain RTP unless equivalent protection is in place, since that would be an effective downgrade.

The SRC and SRS MUST implement TLS mutual authentication for the RS, although using it is a deployment decision. Not authenticating the SRS risks sending a sensitive recording to an attacker, and not authenticating the SRC risks forged recordings. The SRC and SRS MUST support RTP/SAVP and RTP/SAVPF, and at a minimum the SDP security descriptions key negotiation mechanism. An SRC that decrypts the CS media and re-encrypts it for the RS MUST use a different key. An SRC that just replicates packets reuses the CS key, and then it MUST protect the keying material in the RS SDP at least as well as the CS does.

Metadata contains sensitive information such as the participants' addresses of record, so it SHOULD be protected by SIPS/TLS. The document also reminds implementers that storage and playback need comparable security, and gives the example of a recording served over an unauthenticated HTTP interface.
sections.eli5: If you lock the door to a conversation, the room where its recording is kept needs a lock that is just as strong. Otherwise a thief could skip the front door and use the back window.
